references.text: Also in [ref:Luk 13:17|Luke 13:17], Jesus' opponents are put to shame and cannot answer when Jesus defends his healing on the Sabbath. Both texts show that they were unable to contradict Jesus' arguments about mercy on the Sabbath.

The immediate context in [ref:Luk 14:3-5|Luke 14:3-5] shows Jesus' question and argument which they could not answer: whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, and whether they themselves would not have lifted up their child or their ox that fell into a pit on the Sabbath.

In [ref:Matt 22:46|Matthew 22:46] it says that no one could answer Jesus a word, and from that day no one dared to ask him any more questions. This shows a recurring pattern where opponents cannot answer Jesus.
In [ref:Matt 12:11-12|Matthew 12:11-12] Jesus uses a similar argument about saving an animal on the Sabbath to defend healing, and the opponents cannot answer.

In [ref:Apg 6:10|Acts 6:10] they could not stand against the wisdom and Spirit with which Stephen spoke. The Greek expression for being unable to stand against (οὐκ ἴσχυον) is related to Luke's wording (οὐκ ἴσχυσαν).

In [ref:Luk 21:15|Luke 21:15] Jesus promises that he will give his disciples words and wisdom which no opponent shall be able to contradict or stand against (ἀντιστῆναι), a theme that echoes the opponents' silence in Luke 14:6.

In [ref:Rom 9:20|Romans 9:20] Paul uses the expression ἀνταποκρινόμενος (to answer back) – the same Greek verb as in Luke 14:6 (ἀνταποκριθῆναι) – to emphasize that a human being cannot answer God back.
In [ref:Job 5:13|Job 5:13] the wise are caught in their own cunning, a principle illustrated in Luke 14:6 where the opponents are trapped by their own logic and cannot argue against Jesus' reasoning.
